the exemplar states the mechanism outright, so this is not an inference: 'deprotonation of Cl4NHPI by pyridine, followed by anodic oxidation, leads to the tetra-chlorophthalimido N-oxyl radical species' (Horn/Baran, Nature 2016, 533, 77-81, p. 81, Fig. 5 discussion). The species that reaches the anode is therefore the DEPROTONATED anion, and the neutral N-OH is regenerated only afterwards, by hydrogen-atom abstraction from the substrate. The paper's own cyclic voltammetry corroborates it under the reaction's own base conditions: 'In the case of NHPI, a reversible redox couple is observed at 0.78 V versus Ag/AgCl in the presence of excess pyridine, whereas Cl4NHPI shows a redox couple at 0.87 V versus Ag/AgCl under identical conditions' (p. 78). A REVERSIBLE couple is the point: oxidising the neutral N-OH would carry a coupled proton loss and show as a chemically irreversible wave, whereas the anion oxidises to the N-oxyl radical with no accompanying bond change. Stoichiometry agrees -- pyridine at 2.0 equiv against a mediator at 0.2 equiv is a tenfold excess. Note the base screen does NOT run on basicity (pyridine 51 pct, 2,6-lutidine 10 pct, collidine 13 pct, Et3N 0 pct, DBU 0 pct), so pyridine was not chosen for being the strongest base; that ordering bears on which base survives the anode, not on whether the mediator is deprotonated, which the CV settles directly.

The bulk is therefore 92.5% neutral acid. Proton transfer between a carboxylic acid and a tertiary amine is essentially diffusion-limited, so the pre-equilibrium re-equilibrates far faster than diffusion across a 100-300 um film: this is a fast CE case in which the limiting current is set by the TOTAL acid, transported almost entirely as the neutral form. Population-weighted z = -0.075, carried as 0.
